1.pericope_label: The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool

schools.summary: Delitzsch lays out the Gospel scene and the two premises the argument rests on; Ellicott catalogues the six candidates for the psalm's subject and refuses to press the phrase 'at my right hand' beyond a mark of honour.
Calvin argues from the Pharisees' silence and from the impossibility that David or any successor could be a priest for ever after a non-Levitical order.

Clarke surveys and dismisses every non-messianic ascription, reports Venema's dual reading, and collects the manuscript variants; Wesley dates the decree from eternity and its execution to the resurrection.

Henry proves the dignity of Christ from David calling him Lord and hears three things in the sitting posture; Spurgeon dwells on the wonder that a mortal ear should overhear the converse of Father and Son.

Augustine works the Gospel question from the other side, insisting that to deny Christ is David's son is to contradict the opening of Matthew, so that the Pharisees answered rightly and the difficulty stands.

debates.question: Of whom does the psalm speak?

positions.summary: Of the Messiah alone. No history mentions a prince to whom it could be literally applied — David's Lord, seated at God's right hand, king from eternity, everlasting priest and judge of all nations.
Lists six proposals — the Messiah, David, Solomon, Hezekiah, Joshua son of Josedech, an Asmonean priest-king — and notes that the second is inconsistent with Davidic authorship.
A divine oracle partly of David's Lord and partly of David himself, delivered soon after the ark was brought home.
Of Christ, on the authority of the Gospel scene, whose force depends on the psalm being both Davidic and prophetico-Messianic.

debates.question: How much may be pressed from 'Sit thou at my right hand'?

positions.summary: Little. The nearest Old Testament parallels make it only a mark of extreme honour, and the psalm later puts the Lord at the right hand of the person addressed, so the position should not be pressed either way.
A great deal: it is a resting posture after his labours, a ruling posture to give law and judgment, and a remaining posture, for he sits like a king for ever.
It implies the possession of the utmost confidence, power and pre-eminence, given to the God-man after the resurrection.

outliers.summary: Collects the manuscript variants, including one that appears to read 'Jehovah said unto Jehovah' for 'unto my Lord', and eight that make 'footstool' a genitive with the Greek and Latin.

themes: The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool.

2.pericope_label: The Lord shall send the rod of thy strength out of Zion: rule thou in the midst of thine enemies. Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power

schools.summary: Delitzsch reads the day of power as a muster of the levy and the people's response as entire cheerful readiness; Ellicott corrects the verb to 'stretch', assigns the command to Jehovah, and rebuilds the dew clause as a picture of young warriors.
Gill makes the rod the gospel sceptre sent out of Zion and runs the day of power from the apostolic age to the moment of each conversion.
Clarke agrees on the gospel but turns the willing people into a long argument against reading irresistible grace here; Wesley reasons that a spiritual kingdom must have a spiritual sceptre.

debates.question: Does 'thy people shall be willing' teach irresistible grace?

positions.summary: No, and the verse has been woefully perverted to that use: free will is as absurd a phrase as bound will, and a man forced to believe does not believe at all. The Hebrew gives 'thy princely' or 'free people'.
The clause describes cheerful readiness at a muster, not compulsion — no army of mercenaries, but men presenting themselves from inward impulse.
It marks the set time of love and life at conversion, when the exceeding greatness of God's power is put forth in regeneration.
The people offer themselves as living sacrifices and freewill offerings, not oxen or sheep.

debates.question: What is 'the dew of thy youth'?

positions.summary: The army: dew was an emblem of multitude, freshness and brightness, so the young warriors come thick and bright as morning dew.
The offspring — the members of the church, more numerous than the drops.

debates.question: Who speaks 'Rule thou in the midst of thine enemies'?

positions.summary: Better taken as a quotation spoken by Jehovah, who seats the monarch beside him, takes his sceptre and stretches it over the nations.
Read straight as the psalmist's description of a kingdom erected and maintained by the gospel among enemies.

outliers.summary: Reports the Jewish tradition that takes the rod literally and identifies it with the same staff held by Jacob, Judah, Moses, Aaron, David and every king of Judah down to the destruction of the temple.

themes: The Lord shall send the rod of thy strength out of Zion: rule thou in the midst of thine enemies.
Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power, in the beauties of holiness from the womb of the morning: thou hast the dew of thy youth.

4.pericope_label: The Lord hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek. The Lord at thy right hand shall strike through kings in the day of his wrath

schools.summary: Delitzsch settles the subject of the fifth verse from the accents and draws the point that the victory is the Lord's through the exalted one; Ellicott corrects 'order' to 'manner' and traces the union of the two offices through Israel's history.
Gill explains the oath from the doubts it was meant to settle — Phinehas's everlasting priesthood, the dignity of the Son, the tribe of Judah — and canvasses three constructions of the fifth verse.

Clarke expounds the double sense of the Hebrew for priest, Calmet's three orders, and the meaning of Melchizedek's name, then follows Venema in hearing an allusion to Abraham's defeat of the four kings; Wesley reduces the oath to its purpose.
Henry prefers to refer the fifth verse back to the dignity of the first, and Spurgeon rests the whole security of the church on an oath without repentance.

debates.question: At whose right hand, and who is addressed, in the fifth verse?

positions.summary: Three constructions are possible — the words spoken to Christ, to the church, or, preferably, to the Father at whose right hand David's Lord sits.

The king is still the person addressed: the word used here is used nowhere else but of God, and the shift from his right hand to his left is only idiom — sitting at the right hand is honour, standing there is protecting might.
The Lord dashes kings in pieces at the right hand of this priest-king; the accents make him the subject, and the victory is his work through the exalted one.
The psalm turns here to David, and the striking through of kings alludes to Abraham's defeat of the four kings in the chapter where Melchizedek appears.

debates.question: How should 'after the order of Melchizedek' be rendered and understood?

positions.summary: Better 'after the manner of' than 'after the order', since the psalmist can have had no intention of contrasting this priesthood with Aaron's — that contrast became natural only once the Aaronic order was doomed.
After his pattern: Melchizedek's was the priesthood of royalty, one of three orders, and the only one not ended with the Jewish polity.
The most ancient and primitive order, and the ground of the church's security, since the commission is sealed by an oath without repentance.

To settle real doubts — whether the Aaronic priesthood was changed, whether the Son could be called a priest, and how one of Judah could be one at all; and for the people's sake more than for Christ's.
To make the priesthood sure and irrevocable.
Because the decree is irresistible, without condition or contingency, with nothing left to the will of man or angel.

outliers.summary: Reads the present tense of 'Thou art' as covering all times at once — thou wast and art and art to come — because the present is the only time with the Lord.

themes: The Lord hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.
The Lord at thy right hand shall strike through kings in the day of his wrath.

6.pericope_label: He shall judge among the heathen, he shall fill the places with the dead bodies... He shall drink of the brook in the way: therefore shall he lift up the head

schools.summary: Ellicott finds a play on words between heathen and corpses, repoints the clause to 'fulness of corpses', and defends the picture of a thirsty warrior pausing at the brook as poetry rather than indignity.
Gill allows both rule and judgment among the Gentiles, names the Papists as the objects of the second, and prefers a victorious sense for the brook over a sense of suffering.

Clarke reads the closing verses first of David, then of Christ and Antichrist, and finally offers his own key to the whole psalm as a war song; Wesley insists such passages are to be taken spiritually and makes the waters afflictions.

debates.question: What is the brook by the way?

positions.summary: Better read of victory — Christ's conquest over sin, Satan, the world and death — since the clause stands surrounded by others speaking only of triumph, though the reading that makes it his sufferings is reported.
A literal refreshment: the victorious leader, faint yet pursuing, pauses at the stream and continues with head erect.
Sore travail and even death in the struggle, the lifted head being the resurrection and ascent to glory.
Afflictions, since waters in scripture frequently signify sufferings, borne before the honour of sitting at the right hand.

debates.question: Who is the head wounded over many countries?

positions.summary: A crushed host over a vast land, the word meaning a band of men, though others understand the chief of a wide country.
Antichrist — a power of very extensive spiritual domination, identified with an Italian archbishop.
The neighbouring kings brought so low as to acknowledge David and pay tribute.
The princes who oppose him, though the passage is to be taken spiritually, according to the nature of Christ's kingdom.

outliers.summary: Offers as his own a key he says no one else has suggested: the psalm is a war song and every phrase in it military — proclamation, ensign, motto, muster of volunteers, regimentals, numbers, victory, judgment, refreshment, and the emperor proclaimed.
Identifies the heathen who are judged with the Papists, the nations angry when the time of wrath is come.

themes: He shall judge among the heathen, he shall fill the places with the dead bodies; he shall wound the heads over many countries.
He shall drink of the brook in the way: therefore shall he lift up the head.
